title: Baseline Prognosis and Treatment Benefit From First-Line Immunotherapy Strategies: Target Trial Emulations Across Advanced Solid Tumors
authors: Orcutt, X.; Nimgaonkar, V.; Chen, K.; Riaz, I.; Cohen, A.; Mamtani, R.; Gomes, M.; Long, Q.; Parikh, R. B.
abstract: BackgroundIn randomized trials, first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy has shown excess early mortality versus chemotherapy- or targeted therapy-containing regimens. ICI monotherapy is often chosen for frail patients because it is perceived as less toxic. Whether treatment benefit varies with baseline prognosis is unknown, as poor-prognosis patients are underrepresented in trials. MethodsUsing the US Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived database, we emulated target trials among 8,688 patients initiating first-line therapy during 2011-2023 across five comparisons: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus pembrolizumab in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; PD-L1 CPS [≥]1 or unknown) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; PD-L1 TPS [≥]50%); carboplatin plus gemcitabine versus pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma; pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer; and ipilimumab plus nivolumab versus BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis was estimated with machine learning models predicting 6-month survival. Overlap-weighted pseudo-observation regression evaluated whether differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) varied with predicted survival. ResultsIn HNSCC, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab did not clearly improve RMST overall (11.5 days; 95% CI, -18.4 to 41.1), but benefit was 102.4 days greater at the 10th versus 90th percentile of predicted survival (95% CI, 40.5 to 164.3; interaction P=.001). Similar gradients favored carboplatin plus gemcitabine over pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma (10th-90th percentile difference, 51.4 days; 95% CI, 4.8 to 98.1; P=.03) and, less certainly, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab in NSCLC (73.7 days; 95% CI, -3.7 to 151.2; P=.06). Higher-risk patients in these cohorts were more often trial-ineligible. ICI-based therapy improved overall RMST in colorectal cancer (difference, 79.7 days; 95% CI, 49.5 to 107.0) and melanoma (68.3 days; 95% CI, 33.9 to 101.9), without clear variation by predicted survival (interaction P=.32 and P=.91). ConclusionsAmong patients with poorer prognosis, chemotherapy-containing regimens were associated with greater benefit than ICI monotherapy in HNSCC and urothelial carcinoma, and possibly NSCLC. ICI-based therapy appeared beneficial across prognosis in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer and BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis may complement tumor biomarkers when selecting first-line immunotherapy strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Poorer baseline prognosis was associated with greater survival benefit from chemotherapy-containing regimens versus pembrolizumab alone in head and neck and urothelial cancers, with a less certain pattern in lung cancer.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings question the assumption that immunotherapy alone necessarily offers better outcomes for patients with poorer prognosis.
method: Emulated five first-line treatment trials using US electronic health records across advanced solid tumors.
Used machine learning to predict baseline 6-month survival.
Applied overlap-weighted regression to assess treatment differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time by prognosis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 8,688 patients treated during 2011–2023, prognosis-related treatment differences were significant in head and neck and urothelial cancers, while immunotherapy improved overall restricted mean survival in colorectal cancer and melanoma without clear variation by prognosis.
infographic.watch_item: This observational treatment-comparison study—not AI drug discovery—may retain residual confounding and does not establish individualized treatment recommendations.
infographic.paper_title: Baseline Prognosis and Treatment Benefit From First-Line Immunotherapy Strategies: Target Trial Emulations Across Advanced Solid Tumors

title: At-home ankle and wrist accelerometry and machine learning capture motor impairment and disease progression in ataxia-telangiectasia
authors: Kulkarni, D. D.; Toivonen, A. R.; Luddy, A.; Reiling, S.; Thornton, J.; Hoche, F.; Gupta, A. S.
abstract: BackgroundAtaxia-telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare, childhood-onset neurodegenerative disorder for which sensitive, age-appropriate motor outcome measures are needed to support emerging clinical trials. Clinician-rated ataxia scales are limited by subjectivity, low granularity, and floor and ceiling effects. We evaluated whether at-home wearable accelerometry, combined with machine-learned composite scores derived from submovement features, captures cross-sectional motor impairment and longitudinal disease progression in A-T. Methods43 children with classic A-T (median age 9.0 years; IQR 5.7-13.4) and 50 age- and sex-matched controls wore GENEActiv accelerometers on the ankle and wrist during one week of natural behavior at home, repeated at 6- to 12-month intervals. From 85 submovement, activity-intensity, and spectral features per sensor site, we trained composite severity models targeting the Brief Ataxia Rating Scale (BARS) gait subscore (ankle) and BARS total score (wrist). FindingsAnkle composite scores correlated strongly with BARS gait (r = 0.88), BARS total (r = 0.88), and caregiver-reported CPCHILD (r = -0.69); wrist composite scores correlated with BARS total (r = 0.88), BARS arm (r = 0.84), and CPCHILD (r = -0.78). Both models discriminated A-T from controls with large effect sizes (ankle Cohens d = 2.28; wrist d = 2.98) and demonstrated excellent within-week reliability (ICC = 0.95 ankle; 0.92 wrist). The ankle composite captured disease progression sensitively (Mean-to-Standard Deviation Ratio [MSDR] = 0.98; p < 0.0001). In a matched subset with both sensor and clinical data, ankle composite slopes significantly captured progression (Wilcoxon vs zero, p = 0.0036), whereas BARS total (p = 0.079) and BARS gait (p = 0.30) did not. InterpretationAt-home ankle-based wearable accelerometry provides a sensitive, interpretable, and ecologically valid measure of motor function and disease progression in A-T and may serve as a candidate outcome measure for clinical trials. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed and Google Scholar for articles published up to September 2026 using the terms "ataxia-telangiectasia", "wearable", "accelerometer", "digital biomarker", and "motor outcome measure". Clinician-rated ataxia scales remain the standard for assessing motor severity in A-T, but are limited by rater subjectivity, low granularity, and age-dependent baseline scores in children. Task-based wearable assessments have shown promise but share the limitations of requiring structured protocols and participant cooperation. At-home wearable accelerometry using submovement analysis had been applied to the wrist in children with A-T in one prior study by our group, demonstrating cross-sectional validity and longitudinal change over one year. Ankle-worn sensors had been used to estimate ataxia severity in children with A-T during a supervised gait assessment, and at-home ankle-based submovement measures and machine-learned composite scores had shown strong sensitivity in adult cerebellar ataxias. However, at-home composite scores and ankle-based measures had not been evaluated in A-T, and no study had compared ankle and wrist sensor sites in a pediatric A-T cohort or assessed longitudinal sensitivity of ankle-derived measures against clinician-rated scales in A-T. Added value of this studyIn an expanded pediatric cohort of 43 children with A-T and 50 controls followed for up to 5.8 years, we show that machine-learned composite scores derived from ankle and wrist accelerometer data collected during natural behavior at home correlate strongly with clinician-rated ataxia severity and caregiver-reported function, distinguish A-T from controls across age groups, and demonstrate high within-week reliability. The ankle composite captured disease progression with higher sensitivity than clinician-rated BARS, including in non-ambulatory individuals, whereas the wrist composite did not reach significance as a longitudinal measure. Both models identified a consistent motor signature of ataxia across upper and lower limbs. Implications of all the available evidencePassive at-home ankle accelerometry combined with submovement-based machine learning provides a sensitive, low-burden, and scalable measure of motor function and disease progression in A-T. This approach could complement clinician-rated scales as an objective outcome measure to increase clinical trial efficiency and provide early evidence for treatment efficacy. The low-cost single-sensor design supports geographically distributed trial enrollment, which is particularly relevant for rare diseases like A-T.

infographic.key_insight: At-home accelerometry combined with machine learning captured motor impairment in children with ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T), with ankle scores also detecting disease progression.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Ankle-based scores may offer a sensitive outcome measure for A-T clinical trials; this study did not evaluate cancer drug discovery.
method: 43 children with classic A-T and 50 matched controls wore ankle and wrist accelerometers at home for one week.
Monitoring was repeated at 6- to 12-month intervals.
Machine-learning models combined 85 features per sensor site to estimate clinician-rated motor severity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Ankle scores correlated with BARS gait ratings (r = 0.88), showed high within-week reliability (ICC = 0.95), and detected progression in a matched subset (p = 0.0036), where BARS changes were not statistically significant.
infographic.watch_item: The relatively small pediatric cohort warrants independent validation before these scores are adopted as clinical-trial outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: At-home ankle and wrist accelerometry and machine learning capture motor impairment and disease progression in ataxia-telangiectasia

title: WITHDRAWN: Predicting Distant Melanoma Metastasis at Diagnosis Using Machine Learning
authors: Kim, J. J. H.; Lee, J. W. Y.; Yuan, H.; Han, C.; Zandigohar, M.; Haber, R.; Tsoukas, M.; Avanaki, K.
abstract: Distant melanoma metastasis at the time of diagnosis is uncommon, but has major implications for patient prognosis and treatment selection. However, few tools can reliably predict the risk of distant metastasis at initial presentation. Here, we developed and evaluated machine learning models to predict distant melanoma metastasis using routinely captured clinicopathologic and demographic variables across all histologic subtypes. Using the National Cancer Institute Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program from 2010-2022, we identified adults aged 20 to 90 years with melanoma as the first and only primary malignancy (n=51,285). Explainable Boosting Machine achieved a strong balance of discrimination and precision (AUROC = 0.947, AUPRC = 0.610, Precision = 0.793, Brier = 0.015). At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 0.843 with consistent performance across cross-validation folds. Clinicopathologic variables, including T stage, Breslow thickness, ulceration, and mitotic activity, contributed the largest share of predictive signal across descriptive, regression-based, and SHAP analyses, with smaller contributions from demographic factors. Decision curve analysis supported clinical utility, showing a net reduction of 88.3 per 100 patients and a standardized net benefit of 0.541. This model could be used to identify patients at sufficiently elevated risk to justify staging PET/CT despite otherwise localized clinical presentation. Cost-consequence analysis further showed that imaging true- and false-positive patients at 85% to 95% sensitivity threshold nearly doubled downstream imaging cost. We deployed the final model as an online calculator to support exploration of individualized risk estimates (https://melanoma-calculator.streamlit.app/).

infographic.key_insight: This withdrawn study reported that machine learning could predict distant melanoma metastasis at diagnosis; it did not investigate cancer drug discovery.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The proposed use was to inform research on staging-imaging selection, not to establish a validated clinical decision tool.
method: Analyzed routinely recorded clinicopathologic and demographic variables from SEER.
Evaluated machine learning models, including an Explainable Boosting Machine.
Examined predictor contributions, decision curves, and imaging costs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 51,285 adults in SEER (2010–2022), the abstract reported AUROC 0.947, AUPRC 0.610, and specificity 0.843 at 90% sensitivity, with consistent cross-validation performance.
infographic.watch_item: The paper is withdrawn, and the abstract reports no independent external validation; its findings and online calculator should not guide patient care.
infographic.paper_title: WITHDRAWN: Predicting Distant Melanoma Metastasis at Diagnosis Using Machine Learning

title: CB-COMIL: interpretable prediction of melanoma immunotherapyresponse from multiplex immunofluorescence whole-slide images
authors: Rana, P.; Gide, T. N.; Adegoke, N.; Mao, Y.; N. Lo, S.; Berkovsky, S.; Coiera, E.; Long, G. V.; Wilmott, J. S.; Liu, S.
abstract: Deep learning models can predict melanoma immunotherapy response but rarely explain predictions biologically. Concept bottleneck models offer interpretable predictions, but have not been applied to multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), and whether their learned concepts reproduce tissue measurements remains unclear. We developed CB-COMIL, which routes mIF predictions through four supervised concepts (immune:tumour ratio, CD8/SOX10 balance, CD68 relative signal and PD-L1 evasion index), decomposing each prediction exactly into concept contributions. Developed on 211 slides and evaluated on 42 slides from an independent, differently acquired test cohort, CB-COMIL achieved macro-F1 0.69 versus 0.67 for an opaque comparator (difference 0.020, 95% CI -0.103 to 0.144). In 41 slides with complete measurements, learned concepts correlated with measured counterparts (Spearman{rho} 0.61-0.76), yet substituting measured values reduced macro-F1 from 0.68 to 0.48. CB-COMIL makes predictions interpretable without detectable performance loss, and our evaluation shows that concepts can faithfully determine predictions without reproducing the corresponding biological measurements.

infographic.key_insight: CB-COMIL explains melanoma immunotherapy-response predictions through four supervised concepts, but these learned concepts are not interchangeable with measured biological values.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This research could support more interpretable immunotherapy-response prediction, but it does not establish readiness for treatment decisions.
method: Analyzes multiplex immunofluorescence whole-slide images using a concept bottleneck model.
Uses immune:tumour ratio, CD8/SOX10 balance, CD68 relative signal and PD-L1 evasion index.
Decomposes each prediction exactly into concept contributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Developed on 211 slides and independently tested on 42, CB-COMIL achieved macro-F1 0.69 versus 0.67 for an opaque comparator (difference 0.020; 95% CI −0.103 to 0.144).

title: LLM-generated patient-friendly discharge letters for newly diagnosed rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases: a prospective feasibility study
authors: Kremer, P.; Klemm, J.; Wallmeier, P.; Holzer, M.-T.; Pauz, J.; Xiong, T.; Koetter, I.; Melderis, S.; Haase, I.; Krusche, M.
abstract: BackgroundA new diagnosis of a rheumatic and musculoskeletal disease (RMD) creates substantial information needs, with medical discharge letters often serving as a primary source of information for patients. This study aimed to assess the feasibility, content quality and patient-reported usefulness of large language model (LLM)-generated patient-friendly discharge letters in rheumatology inpatient care. MethodsIn this prospective, single-centre, single-arm feasibility study, standard discharge letters were transformed into patient-friendly versions using GPT models, reviewed by treating physicians and provided alongside the originals. We assessed physician review time, corrections, information fidelity, readability, understandability and patient-reported evaluations at follow-up. ResultsOf 58 enrolled patients, 52 (89.7%) completed follow-up. Compared with the original letters, patient-friendly letters showed significantly higher Flesch Reading Ease scores (mean difference 11.4, 95% confidence interval 9.8 to 12.9) and higher understandability scores on the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (+10.0 percentage points, 95% confidence interval 6.8 to 13.4). Physicians rated all 58 unedited drafts as "very good" or "good", and review took less than five minutes for 43/58 (74.1%) letters. Unedited LLM drafts contained eleven medical discrepancies in 10/58 (17.2%) letters, ten of which were corrected before discharge. In the final physician-reviewed letters, 310/311 (99.7%) applicable letter-domain assessments were classified as correctly retained or simplified. At follow-up, 42/51 (82.4%) patients rated perceived comparative comprehensibility favourably and 44/51 (86.3%) wished to receive similar letters in future. ConclusionsPhysician-reviewed, LLM-generated discharge letters were feasible to implement in routine rheumatology care, with limited physician review time and high patient acceptance. Although text-based readability and assessed understandability improved, objective patient comprehension and clinical benefit remain to be established. Discrepancies in unedited drafts underscore the need for physician oversight. Trial registrationGerman Clinical Trials Register (DRKS), DRKS00036980. Registered 26 May 2025.

infographic.key_insight: In this rheumatology study—not cancer drug discovery—physician-reviewed, LLM-generated discharge letters improved readability and assessed understandability compared with standard letters.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patient-friendly letters may support communication after a new rheumatic or musculoskeletal diagnosis, but improved patient comprehension and clinical outcomes remain unproven.
method: Prospective, single-centre, single-arm feasibility study enrolling 58 patients.
GPT models simplified standard discharge letters; physicians reviewed drafts before patients received both versions.
Evaluated review time, medical discrepancies, information fidelity, readability and patient feedback.
infographic.evidence_signal: Readability increased by 11.4 Flesch points and assessed understandability by 10.0 percentage points; 44/51 follow-up respondents (86.3%) wanted similar letters in future.
infographic.watch_item: Unedited drafts contained 11 medical discrepancies across 10/58 letters; ten discrepancies were corrected before discharge, underscoring the need for physician oversight.
infographic.paper_title: LLM-generated patient-friendly discharge letters for newly diagnosed rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases: a prospective feasibility study

title: Plasma DNA fragmentomic analysis for evaluation of patients with pancreatic cystic neoplasms
authors: Marcinak, C. T.; Stephens, M. D.; Chen, J.; Merali, N.; McDonald, B. R.; Dietmann, E. C.; Nawaz, M. T.; McGregor, S. M.; Ronnekleiv-Kelly, S. M.; Weber, S. M.; Nkadori, E. N.; Stadmeyer, P. G.; Benson, M. E.; Gopal, D. V.; Zafar, S. N.; Kelly, K. J.; Mathew, J.; Pirasteh, A.; Frampton, A. E.; Pfau, P. R.; Sivakumar, S.; Minter, R. M.; Murtaza, M.
abstract: BackgroundIncidental detection of pancreatic cystic neoplasms (PCNs) is common, but to identify patients with malignant PCNs (high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma) who need invasive testing such as endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) or surgery is challenging. Plasma DNA fragmentomic analysis has recently shown promise for early detection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). ObjectiveTo evaluate the ability of plasma DNA fragmentomic analysis to differentiate between patients with benign and malignant PCNs. DesignWe performed whole genome sequencing of pre-treatment plasma DNA from 121 patients with PDAC, 121 age and sex-matched healthy controls, and 99 patients with PCNs referred for EUS (total n=341). After training and validating a plasma DNA fragmentomics machine learning model for PDAC detection, we independently evaluated its performance for detection of malignant PCNs, and compared with circulating glycoproteins. ResultsEleven of 99 patients (11%) were diagnosed with malignant PCNs during 24.6 months of clinical follow-up. For PDAC detection, plasma DNA analysis showed area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.97. For malignant PCN detection, plasma DNA analysis showed AUROC of 0.67, while CA19-9, CA125 and CEA showed AUROCs of 0.78, 0.54, and 0.63, respectively. Combined analysis of plasma DNA with glycoproteins showed AUROC of 0.92, demonstrating 91% sensitivity, 99% negative predictive value, 88% specificity and 48% positive predictive value for malignant PCN detection. ConclusionPlasma DNA fragmentomics and glycoprotein biomarkers showed complementary performance for detecting malignant PCNs in patients referred for EUS. This approach could improve patient selection for EUS, and warrants further evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: Combining plasma DNA fragmentomics with glycoprotein biomarkers distinguished malignant from benign pancreatic cystic neoplasms with an AUROC of 0.92.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This diagnostic biomarker approach—not a drug discovery study—could help refine selection for endoscopic ultrasound, pending further validation.
method: Performed whole-genome sequencing of pretreatment plasma DNA from 341 participants.
Trained and validated a machine-learning fragmentomics model using 121 pancreatic cancer patients and 121 matched healthy controls.
Independently evaluated 99 patients with pancreatic cystic neoplasms, comparing and combining fragmentomics with glycoprotein biomarkers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 99 cyst patients, 11 had malignant disease during 24.6 months of follow-up; combined biomarkers achieved 91% sensitivity, 88% specificity, 99% negative predictive value and 48% positive predictive value.
infographic.watch_item: Only 11 malignant cyst cases were evaluated in an endoscopic-ultrasound referral cohort, limiting precision and generalizability to broader screening populations.
infographic.paper_title: Plasma DNA fragmentomic analysis for evaluation of patients with pancreatic cystic neoplasms

title: Mechanistic Assessment of Norepinephrine Therapy versus Angiotensin-II on Organ Function in Septic Shock (MANTRA): Study Protocol for a multicenter open-label randomized trial
authors: Filbin, M.; Leisman, D. E.; Pachano-Bravo, A.; Goldberg, M. B.; Hibbert, K. A.; Nelson, O.; Rappaport, B.; Mahler, S. A.; Harris, L.; Besong, E. B.; Reeves, B.; Maves, R. C.; Petrilli, A.; Schaich, C. L.; Files, D. C.; Gibbs, K.; Chappell, M. C.; Khanna, A. K.
abstract: IntroductionNorepinephrine remains first-line vasopressor therapy for septic shock despite its association at high doses with undesirable cardiovascular, kidney, and immune effects. Angiotensin-II (Ang-II) is a non-catecholamine vasopressor of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) now approved to increase blood pressure in vasodilatory shock. RAAS dysregulation is common in septic shock and may represent a treatable trait. However, few prospective investigations evaluate the effect of early Ang-II use in septic shock on dysfunctional RAAS biology, host-response, or clinical outcomes. Therefore, we designed a mechanistic clinical trial to test the hypothesis that early Ang-II therapy in septic shock normalizes systemic RAAS abnormalities and modulates innate immune responses. Methods and AnalysisThe Mechanistic Assessment of Norepinephrine TheRapy vs. Angiotensin-II in Septic Shock (MANTRA) trial is an investigator-initiated, prospective, multicenter, open-label, randomized mechanistic clinical trial. Adults with septic shock by Sepsis-3 criteria receiving a norepinephrine-equivalent dose (NED) of 0.10-0.50 mcg/kg/min will be randomized 1:1 to primary Ang-II (to a maximum 40 ng/kg/min) or norepinephrine (to a maximum 35 mcg/min) treatment strategies over a 48-hour period. The primary outcome is the between-group difference in plasma renin trajectory from baseline to 24 hours represented as a treatment-by-time interaction term in a linear mixed-effects model. With n=78, the trial has 90% power (at two-sided =0.05) to detect a 25% between-group difference in 24-hour renin. Secondary clinical outcomes include longitudinal NED, hours alive and vasopressor-free at 72 hours, a 28-day composite outcome (days alive and free of vasopressors, renal replacement therapy, and mechanical ventilation), treatment failure requiring crossover or protocol discontinuation, and thrombotic and arrhythmia events through 28 days. Secondary mechanistic outcomes include serial RAAS biomarkers (prorenin, soluble prorenin receptor, angiotensinogen, ACE, ACE2, Ang-II, angiotensin-(1-7), aldosterone, and DPP3), immune measures (ex vivo monocyte function, monocyte gene expression, plasma cytokines), and organ injury biomarkers. Enrollment is planned from 11/2026-7/2030. Ethics and DisseminationThe study has been approved by the Advocate Health/Wake Forest University School of Medicine ethics commitee (IRB00115287). Informed consent is required. Results will be submitted for publication in peer-reviewed journals and presented at national and international scientific meetings, regardless of the direction of findings. Results will be posted to ClinicalTrials.gov. Trial RegistrationClinicaltrials.gov - NCT06746753 Administrative InformationThis manuscript has been written in accordance with the SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) guidelines. The administrative information is described in Table 1. title: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data
authors: Gutierrez-Alvarez, I.; Rojas, A.; Calzadilla-Bertot, L.; Dopazo, J.; Romero-Gomez, M.; Loucera, C.
abstract: BackgroundShort-term prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhosis is complicated by the competing risk of death from liver disease. We aimed to develop an interpretable model on region-wide routine data that predicts HCC while separating competing mortality, and to compare it with established risk scores. MethodsFrom a region-wide cohort of adults with cirrhosis in the Andalusian Population Health Database, we trained the model on 17,177 patients with a prediction date set 12 months before their outcome, between 2020 and 2023. From one year of electronic health records before that date (demographics, liver and chronic disease codes, and eight routine laboratory tests), an Explainable Boosting Machine without interaction terms classified the following 12 months as HCC, death or liver transplantation without HCC, or event-free. We evaluated it in 20 repeats of 5-fold cross-validation against a binary model, a model with pair interactions and a model using the full health record, all on the same folds. We then applied the cross-validated models, without retraining, at the first routine encounter at which aMAP or the Toronto HCC Risk Index could be computed, and compared them with the scores in patients followed forward under competing risks, with and without a 6-month washout and with each province left out of training in turn. Findings771 patients (4.5%) developed HCC within 12 months and 3,314 (19.3%) died or underwent liver transplantation without HCC (3,061 deaths, 253 transplants). In cross-validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for HCC was 0.734 (SD 0.018). A binary formulation, pairwise interactions and the full health record (more than 3,000 features) did not improve it; the full record lowered it by 0.024. At routine encounters the model discriminated 12-month HCC better than aMAP (time-dependent AUC 0.790 vs 0.688; difference +0.102, 95% CI +0.071 to +0.132) and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (0.761 vs 0.703; +0.057, +0.032 to +0.081), and remained better after excluding HCC diagnosed within 6 months (concordance difference +0.055 and +0.040) and when each of the eight provinces was left out of training. At equal group size, its high-risk group held as much HCC as the scores high-risk categories, with 20-28% fewer competing deaths. Its shape functions separated cancer-specific signal (AFP rising from 2 to 20 {micro}g/L, platelets below 150 x109/L) from liver failure (bilirubin above 51 {micro}mol/L, albumin below 35 g/L); a binary model showed only the first. InterpretationAn interpretable three-class model on routine data outperformed established scores for short-term HCC risk in cirrhosis, while showing whether each abnormal value points to cancer or to competing death. FundingThis work was supported by grants PID2023_152380OB and PRTR-C17.I1 from the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation; grant PMP24/00005 from the Instituto de Salud Carlos III (ISCIII); grant IE19_259 FPS from Consejeria de Salud y Consumo, Junta de Andalucia; and Horizon Europe (HORIZON), Marie Skodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Networks (101226456-MLCARE). The funders had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation or writing of the report. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed to October 2026 for HCC risk prediction in cirrhosis with machine learning or risk scores. Machine-learning models usually outperform aMAP and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (THRI) in development data. They are mostly specific to one etiology (HBV or HCV), built on inputs not routinely available (elastography), black boxes explained post hoc, and evaluated without competing risks. A meta-analysis of models for non-viral liver disease found only one developed with a competing-risk approach, and rated all 14 included studies at high risk of bias (1). In prospective French cohorts analysed under competing risks, machine learning did not outperform aMAP (2). Added value of this studyIn a region-wide population of 17,177 adults with cirrhosis of all etiologies, we developed an interpretable three-class model on routine records: HCC, death or transplant, or event-free. Under competing risks, at the first encounter where each score could be computed, it ranked HCC better than aMAP and THRI, including after a 6-month washout. At the same group size it flagged as much HCC with 20-28% fewer patients who died first. The advantage held when each province was left out of training. Its shape functions are the whole model, not a post-hoc approximation, and separate markers of cancer from markers of liver failure. A binary model on the same data ranks HCC as well but folds the death signal into its single curve, as we show analytically. Implications of all the available evidenceSurveillance programmes can rank patients from data they already hold, with a model whose every contribution can be inspected. Modelling death as an outcome keeps patients unlikely to benefit off the high-risk list. External validation in other health systems, with local recalibration, is the next step.

infographic.key_insight: An interpretable AI model predicted 12-month liver cancer risk in people with cirrhosis better than established scores while distinguishing cancer from competing death or transplantation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The model could support research into risk-stratified hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance, but clinical benefit has not been established.
method: Trained an Explainable Boosting Machine on 17,177 adults with cirrhosis using demographics, diagnosis codes and eight routine laboratory tests.
Predicted three outcomes: hepatocellular carcinoma, death or liver transplantation without cancer, and event-free survival.
Used repeated cross-validation and routine-encounter comparisons with aMAP and the Toronto HCC Risk Index.
infographic.evidence_signal: Cross-validation HCC AUROC was 0.734; routine-encounter 12-month AUC was 0.790 versus 0.688 for aMAP and 0.761 versus 0.703 for the Toronto score in their respective comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: The supplied abstract is truncated; reported validation is within Andalusia, leaving generalizability and prospective clinical utility uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data

title: Disease-specific versus symptom-specific neuroimaging phenotypes across Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Small Vessel Disease
authors: Lazari, A.; Broulidakis, J.; Gillis, G.; Bhalerao, G.; Halls, D.; Wickham, F.; Tendler, B. C.; Sotiropoulos, S. N.; Griffanti, L.; Husain, M.; Mars, R. B.
abstract: BackgroundNeurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems. MethodsWe collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimers Disease, Parkinsons Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity. ResultsWe replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimers Disease, Parkinsons Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses. ConclusionsThese results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

infographic.key_insight: Across Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and small vessel disease, MRI revealed both diagnosis-specific brain changes and shared features associated with cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings may help researchers understand symptom heterogeneity across neurological disorders, but do not establish clinically validated biomarkers.
method: Studied 251 participants spanning three disease groups and age-matched healthy controls.
Combined harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessments with multimodal MRI using the UK Biobank protocol.
Compared diagnosis-specific imaging features and symptom–brain associations across diagnoses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study replicated established case–control brain differences and linked lower medial frontal pole–motor cortex connectivity to apathy, fatigue, and depression, while cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses.
infographic.watch_item: The reported associations do not establish causality; this study concerns neurodegeneration, not AI-driven cancer drug discovery.
infographic.paper_title: Disease-specific versus symptom-specific neuroimaging phenotypes across Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Small Vessel Disease

title: The EEG-Respiratory Gap: a deep learning biomarker associated with long-term mortality in obstructive sleep apnea
authors: Lee, H. K.; Park, K.; Choi, Y. R.; Lee, D.-e.; Kim, H.-S.; Shin, H.-W.
abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) summarizes respiratory events by frequency, but was not designed to reflect how strongly an individuals brain responds to them. We developed a deep-learning model that estimates AHI from a single EEG channel (AHIbrain), developed using 22,044 polysomnography recordings and validated in an internal test set (r = 0.88) and three external test sets (r = 0.50-0.62). From AHIbrain, we derived two complementary metrics that characterize the EEG-Respiratory Gap: {Delta}AHIbrain, reflecting whether a patients AHIbrain is higher or lower than expected for their measured AHI, and AHIbrain,event-free, estimated from epochs without scored respiratory events. Both were associated with sleep macro-, micro-, and epoch-level EEG features, suggesting that this discrepancy is not solely attributable to model error. Among participants free of cardiovascular disease, both metrics were associated with all-cause and non-CVD mortality after adjustment for AHI and clinical risk factors. After accounting for the same covariates, AHIbrain,event-free was also associated with CVD mortality in the highest-versus-lowest quartile comparison. These findings support the EEG-Respiratory Gap as an interpretable EEG-derived measure associated with prognostic information beyond AHI.

infographic.key_insight: In obstructive sleep apnea, the EEG-Respiratory Gap captures differences between EEG-derived and measured respiratory-event burden associated with long-term mortality beyond AHI.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These EEG-derived metrics may offer prognostic information beyond respiratory-event frequency, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Developed a deep-learning model to estimate AHI from a single EEG channel.
Calculated ΔAHIbrain to reflect EEG-derived AHI above or below expectations for measured AHI.
Estimated AHIbrain,event-free from epochs without scored respiratory events.
infographic.evidence_signal: Developed using 22,044 sleep recordings, the model correlated with measured AHI internally (r = 0.88) and across three external test sets (r = 0.50–0.62); both gap metrics were associated with all-cause and non-CVD mortality among participants initially free of CVD after adjustment for AHI and clinical risk factors.
infographic.watch_item: Lower external correlations raise generalizability concerns, and mortality associations do not establish causality or clinical benefit.
infographic.paper_title: The EEG-Respiratory Gap: a deep learning biomarker associated with long-term mortality in obstructive sleep apnea

title: Spatially localized racial differences in the association between white matter hyperintensities and verbal memory in cognitively unimpaired adults
authors: Wu, J.; Lin, Q.; James, T. A.; Levey, A. I.; Lah, J. J.; Qiu, D.; The HABS-HD Study Team,
abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are common in aging, but whether their cognitive associations differ between African American and White older adults is unclear. We studied 5,187 cognitively unimpaired non-Hispanic African American (NHA) and non-Hispanic White (NHW) older adults across three independent cohorts using depth- and lobe-resolved WMH mapping with cross-sectional, longitudinal and machine learning analyses. In the Emory Healthy Brain Study (EHBS), greater WMH burden was more strongly associated with poorer verbal memory among NHA than NHW participants. A similar difference was observed in a 34-center cohort but not detected in the third cohort. Differences localized to frontal juxtacortical and parietal deep white matter in EHBS and the multicenter cohort, respectively, and did not parallel WMH burden distributions. Estimates changed little after adjustment for cohort-specific Alzheimers disease (AD) biomarkers, vascular risk factors, structural imaging measures and APOE genotype. Accounting for neighborhood deprivation in EHBS yielded a similar estimate. Generalized random forests supported these differences without assuming a linear interaction. Baseline frontal juxtacortical WMH burden showed a stronger association with subsequent AD-signature cortical thinning among NHA than NHW participants in EHBS, with directionally similar multicenter findings. Spatially resolved WMH measures may help identify early heterogeneity in vascular contributions to cognitive aging.

infographic.key_insight: White matter hyperintensities showed stronger associations with poorer verbal memory in non-Hispanic African American than non-Hispanic White older adults in two of three cohorts, with differences localized to specific white matter regions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Spatially resolved white matter measures may help characterize vascular contributions to cognitive aging, but these findings do not establish clinical utility or race-based care recommendations.
method: Mapped white matter hyperintensities by depth and brain lobe across three independent cohorts.
Used cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses plus generalized random forests.
Adjusted for cohort-specific Alzheimer’s biomarkers, vascular risks, structural imaging measures and APOE genotype.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 5,187 cognitively unimpaired older adults, group differences appeared in EHBS and a 34-center cohort but were not detected in the third cohort; implicated regions also differed between cohorts.
infographic.watch_item: Observational associations and inconsistent replication limit causal interpretation; racial categories should not be treated as biological mechanisms.
infographic.paper_title: Spatially localized racial differences in the association between white matter hyperintensities and verbal memory in cognitively unimpaired adults

title: Bacterial Sexually Transmitted Infections and Oral HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis Use in HVTN 704/HPTN 085
authors: Gallardo-Cartagena, J. A.; Hunidzarira, P.; Gillespie, K.; Juraska, M.; Veloso, V.; Edupuganti, S.; Konda, K.; Roxby, A.; Cohen, M.; Corey, L.; Karuna, S.; Sanchez, J.
abstract: ObjectivesTo describe bacterial STI burden and examine its association with time-varying oral PrEP use among participants in a multinational HIV prevention efficacy trial. MethodsWe conducted a post-hoc analysis of HVTN 704/HPTN 085 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02716675), a randomized, placebo-controlled study of the VRC01 broadly neutralizing antibody for HIV prevention. Men and transgender persons who have sex with men were enrolled in Brazil, Peru, United States, and Switzerland (April 2016-October 2018). All participants received an enhanced prevention package including STI testing every six months and optional access to oral PrEP. Prevalence and incidence of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis were described. Cox proportional hazards models estimated associations between time-varying PrEP use and incident STIs. ResultsAmong 2,687 participants, 27.9% had a bacterial STI at enrollment (chlamydia 11.1%, gonorrhea 10.2%, syphilis 13.1%). Prevalence was higher in Brazil (36.7%) and Peru (34.9%) than in the United States/Switzerland (21.4%). Rectal and oropharyngeal infections predominated. Among participants negative at baseline, incidence of any bacterial STI was 29.4 per 100 person-years (95% CI: 27.2-31.7). Incidence was higher during periods of PrEP use than non-use (HR 1.75, 95% CI: 1.44-2.13), consistent across pathogens. ConclusionsIn this multinational HIV prevention trial, bacterial STI burden was high, particularly in Latin America and at extragenital sites. STI incidence was higher during periods of reported oral PrEP use. These findings highlight the importance of integrating multisite STI testing, treatment, counseling, and targeted prevention into HIV prevention services and future efficacy trials. SummaryParticipants in HVTN 704/HPTN 085 had high bacterial STI burden, especially in Latin America. Incidence was higher while on PrEP, highlighting need for integrated STI prevention within HIV prevention programs.

infographic.key_insight: In HVTN 704/HPTN 085, bacterial STI burden was high, and reported oral PrEP use was associated with higher STI incidence.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings support integrating multisite STI testing, treatment, counseling, and targeted prevention into HIV prevention services.
method: Post-hoc analysis of 2,687 men and transgender persons who have sex with men across four countries.
STI testing every six months, with optional access to oral PrEP.
Cox models examined associations between time-varying PrEP use and incident bacterial STIs.
infographic.evidence_signal: At enrollment, 27.9% had a bacterial STI; among those negative at baseline, incidence was 29.4 per 100 person-years, with higher incidence during PrEP use than non-use (HR 1.75; 95% CI 1.44–2.13).
infographic.watch_item: PrEP use was not randomized, so this association does not establish that PrEP caused higher STI incidence; this paper concerns HIV/STI prevention, not AI cancer drug discovery.
infographic.paper_title: Bacterial Sexually Transmitted Infections and Oral HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis Use in HVTN 704/HPTN 085
